attempts.label: CRCNS:vim-2
attempts.entry_title: Motion-energy encoding of natural movies in human visual cortex (Nishimoto et al. 2011)
attempts.summary: The paper's encoding findings held up in this data, while its movie reconstructions could not be tested. Motion-energy models predicted visual cortex responses better than a static model, with a small gain from direction, V1 best predicted, retinotopic receptive fields and faster preferred speeds in the periphery. The model identified the test second behind 88% of one subject's responses, against the paper's 95%. Both results rest on ridge regression in place of the paper's L1 fit, whose penalty choice the paper does not give, and hold only with penalties chosen by cross-validation. Reconstruction and identification among a million clips need a library of internet movies that is not public.
attempts.description: Tests the encoding-model findings of Nishimoto, Vu, Naselaris, Benjamini, Yu and Gallant (2011) on CRCNS vim-2, which holds the BOLD responses of three subjects to 7,200 s of training movies and 540 s of test movies repeated ten times, with the movies themselves. It fits static, nondirectional and directional motion-energy models to the voxels of V1 to V3B, compares their prediction accuracy by subject and area, maps receptive fields and speed tuning with simulated probes, identifies the test second that evoked each BOLD pattern in subject S1, and tests a model with color channels. The sampled movie prior and the 1,000,000-clip set used for reconstruction are not public.

outcomes.statement: Averaged over subjects and voxels in V1, V2, V3, V3A and V3B, the prediction accuracy on the test data is 0.24 for the static model, 0.39 for the nondirectional motion-energy model and 0.40 for the directional motion-energy model, and the differences are significant (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.0001).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 6; Figures 2D and 2E with legend
outcomes.quote: The averaged accuracy across subjects and voxels in early visual areas (V1, V2, V3, V3A, and V3B) was 0.24, 0.39, and 0.40 for the static, nondirectional, and directional encoding models, respectively ... difference in prediction accuracy was significant (p < 0.0001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test)

statistics.about: directional against nondirectional and static models, voxel-wise
statistics.n: voxels of V1, V2, V3, V3A and V3B in three subjects

outcomes.notes: Under penalty reading b (five-fold cross-validation) with the repeat-averaged test signal (signal reading a), the pooled means over 13,007 voxels are 0.233 (static), 0.384 (nondirectional) and 0.386 (directional), all within tolerance, in the paper's order, with paired two-sided Wilcoxon p below 0.0001 (directional against nondirectional 1.3e-22, against static printed as 0). The mean of subject means gives 0.234, 0.384 and 0.386. Under penalty reading a (one held-out 10%) the means are 0.211, 0.370 and 0.373, with the same order and tests, but the static mean is 0.005 below its lower bound of 0.216; that reading alone would give partially reproduced. Per subject, penalty and signal reading a, S1 0.217, 0.376, 0.376; S2 0.197, 0.391, 0.397; S3 0.221, 0.342, 0.345. Single repeats (signal reading b) give 0.118 to 0.128 (static) and 0.207 to 0.212 (directional), outside tolerance under both penalty readings. The stored rv gives the same means as the z-scored repeats to within 0.003. The outcome rests on ridge in place of L1 and on penalty reading b. An approximate L1 fit on 120 voxels (40 per subject, at random) predicts better than ridge on the same voxels, static 0.243 against 0.218 (reading a) and 0.238 (reading b), directional 0.416 against 0.391 and 0.405; shifting the static mean of all voxels by the subsample's difference gives 0.236 (reading a) and 0.238 (reading b), both inside tolerance. This check suggests the outcome does not hinge on ridge or on the penalty reading; it is a subsample, and the outcome does not rest on it.
deviations: Ridge regression replaces the paper's L1-regularized least squares (Supplemental, Model Fitting, "L1-regularized least squares regression procedure was used to obtain the linear weights", refs. 15 and 16). This is an assumption. The paper gives neither the L1 penalty nor the stopping rule of its coordinate descent, and ridge with a penalty per voxel chosen on held-out data is the standard fit of voxel-wise encoding models of this kind. As a check, the static and directional models are fit by an approximate L1 (accelerated proximal gradient along seven penalties from 0.5 to 0.01 of the largest useful one, 60 iterations each, penalty chosen per voxel on the held-out 10%) on 120 voxels; the paper gives no stopping rule, and at the smallest penalties the objective still changes by about 1% over the last iterations. The penalty is chosen per voxel from 19 values (1 to 1e9, half decades) under both readings of the claims file, (a) a held-out 10% of the training data in 50 s blocks and (b) five-fold cross-validation over such blocks (whole decades only, for time), and the model is refit on all training data.

The data set's test responses are not on the scale of the z-scored training responses (s.d. 0.10 for rv and 0.20 for rva, against 0.99 for rt). Each test repeat is z-scored per voxel before averaging, following Data Preprocessing ("For each 10 minute run and each individual voxel ... signals were then normalized to mean 0.0 and standard deviation 1.0"). Correlations with the mean signal hardly depend on this.
Voxels are those of the data set's V1, V2, V3, V3A and V3B masks (4,183, 4,668 and 4,410 per subject, against the paper's about 4,500); 179, 46 and 29 voxels with missing values are dropped.

The motion-energy bank is pymoten's pyramid with spatial frequencies 0 to 32 cycles/image on 96 x 96 frames at 15 Hz, which gives exactly 6,555 filters (spatial envelope 0.6 wavelengths, 10-frame window), the reading the claims file asks to reproduce that count. Its 855 zero-spatial-frequency filters are one per position of each nonzero frequency's grid, with that frequency's envelope, at each temporal frequency, and have no direction ("zero spatial frequency filters occur only once (no orientation)", Gabor Wavelet Basis Set); the nondirectional model keeps them as single features, so it has 4,275 features. Quadrature pairs are combined by the square root of the summed squares before the log, which after the z-score differs from the paper's squared sum only through the log offset of 1e-5. The log is pymoten's log(x + 1e-5), which is the claims file's log(x) reading, not its standard choice log(1 + x); the claims file judges this unlikely to change the outcome, and log(1 + x) was not run. Envelope variants (half and double) were not run, for time.

The held-out 10% and the five folds are drawn once and used for all three subjects, so that one eigendecomposition of the kernel serves the three (standard choice); the held-out blocks are laid on the concatenated kept samples, and hold 728 samples.

outcomes.statement: The directional model predicts better than the nondirectional model, but the difference is small, which suggests that BOLD signals carry spatially localized but mostly nondirectional motion information.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 6; Figure 2E with legend; Figure S1A
outcomes.quote: Note that the difference in prediction accuracy between the directional and nondirectional motion models, though significant, was small
outcomes.notes: Directional minus nondirectional accuracy is 0.0010 to 0.0034 against a nondirectional gain over static of 0.083 to 0.159, ratios of 0.012 to 0.022, under the bound of 0.1, with Wilcoxon p below 0.0001 (largest 5.2e-22), under every reading of penalty, test signal and subject combination. The directional model is better in 53%, 62% and 55% of voxels of S1, S2 and S3. Whether this shows that BOLD signals carry mostly nondirectional information, as the statement suggests, is an interpretation the criterion does not test. The criterion is pooled; per subject, S1 has a difference of 0.0003 with p = 2.1e-03, which would not pass p < 0.0001 alone.
deviations: The fits of fig2de-prediction-accuracy, with its deviations (ridge in place of L1).

outcomes.statement: In each of the five visual areas and each of the three subjects, both motion models predict better than the static model, and the best predictions are in V1 for all three subjects (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p < 0.0001).
outcomes.quote: The directional and non-directional motion models perform better than the static model in every case. The best overall predictions for all three subjects (p < 0.0001, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) are obtained in area V1.

statistics.n: voxels per area, each of three subjects

outcomes.notes: Both motion models beat the static model in 15 of 15 area and subject cells under both test-signal readings. V1 has the highest mean accuracy in each subject for each model. Against the other four areas pooled (rank-sum reading b), V1 is better with p below 0.0001 in all three subjects for every model, one-sided or two-sided (largest two-sided p 2.8e-10, S3 directional). Against each other area in turn (reading a), this holds in all three subjects for the static model, in two for the nondirectional model and in one for the directional model. Every failure is V1 against V3A, nondirectional in S3 (one-sided p = 1.2e-02) and directional in S1 (4.1e-04) and S3 (3.8e-02); in S2 both motion models pass against every area (largest one-sided p 8.2e-06, V1 against V2, directional). The criterion is met under rank-sum reading b with either model reading, and under reading a with the static model; doubling the one-sided p-values changes no pass or fail.
deviations: The fits of fig2de-prediction-accuracy, with its deviations (ridge in place of L1), under penalty reading a.
The rank-sum p-values are given one-sided (V1 greater, as the claim is that V1 is best) and two-sided; both give the same counts.

outcomes.statement: Voxel receptive fields estimated from the motion-energy model are spatially localized and retinotopically organized; their angle maps are similar to those from conventional multifocal mapping, and their eccentricity maps are similar except in the far periphery, where the multifocal mapping stimulus was coarse.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 7; Figures 2F to 2I with legends
outcomes.quote: The spatial receptive fields of individual voxels were spatially localized (Figures 2F and 2G, left) and were organized retinotopically (Figures 2H and 2I)
outcomes.notes: On the claims file's proxy test, which replaces the multifocal maps the data set does not hold. Retained voxels (prediction p <= 0.01 on the 486 test samples, reading a) are 3,037, 3,867 and 3,358 in S1, S2 and S3, of which 97%, 95% and 95% have a Gaussian fit centered inside the display (bound over half). The centers of left-hemisphere V1 voxels lie in the right visual field in 90%, 91% and 84% of cases, those of right-hemisphere V1 voxels in the left field in 91%, 89% and 89% (bound over 75%). V1 eccentricity rises from the occipital pole forward, Pearson r = 0.535, 0.607 and 0.330 (p = 2.6e-61, 7.3e-89, 2.9e-27; bound p < 0.05). Reading b of the p-value (the 728 held-out training samples) passes as well in every subject (contralateral 0.86 to 0.92, r = 0.312 to 0.607). The forward direction is that from the V1 masks to the MT masks along the slice axis (mean slice 8.7 to 9.9 against 3.4 to 4.3). The similarity of the maps to multifocal mapping, which the statement also asserts, could not be tested: the mapping data are not in the data set and not public.
deviations: Probes follow Selectivity Estimation (17 x 17 grid of dynamic Gaussian white noise on uniform gray; full-field drifting gratings at the basis set's six spatial frequencies, three temporal frequencies and eight directions; response minus the response to gray). The paper does not give the noise or grating contrast, the gray level or the probe duration; the standard choices are L* 50 gray, noise s.d. 25 L*, grating amplitude 40 L*, 40 frames of which the middle 20 are scored. The predicted response to a sustained probe is its features times the directional weights (penalty reading a) summed over the four delays. The Gaussian is isotropic, fit by a search over centers (half-cell steps, also outside the display) and widths with amplitude and offset by least squares.

Judged on the claims file's proxy test (fits inside the display, contralateral V1, eccentricity rising forward along V1); the comparison with multifocal maps is not run, since those maps are not public.
The fits of fig2de-prediction-accuracy (ridge in place of L1), under penalty reading a.

outcomes.statement: Optimal speed (peak temporal frequency over peak spatial frequency) correlates positively with eccentricity, so peripheral voxels prefer higher speeds, in V1, V2 and V3 of all three subjects (t test for correlation coefficient, p < 0.0001).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 8; Figure 2J; Figure S1B legend
outcomes.quote: Projecting the optimal speed of the voxels onto a flattened map of the cortical surface (Figure 2J) revealed a significant positive correlation between eccentricity and optimal speed ... This pattern was observed in areas V1, V2, and V3 and for all three subjects (p < 0.0001, t test for correlation coefficient

statistics.n: voxels of each of V1, V2 and V3 in each of three subjects

outcomes.notes: Under both peak readings (joint map, marginal curves) and both p-value readings, optimal speed correlates positively with eccentricity in all nine area and subject cells with p < 0.0001. Joint peaks with p-value reading a give r = 0.216 to 0.450 over 735 to 1,268 voxels per cell (largest p 1.0e-12, S2 V3); marginal peaks give r = 0.209 to 0.390 (largest p 2.8e-11). Voxels with optimal spatial frequency 0 (4 to 20 per cell) are left out; eccentricity is that of fits centered inside the display.
deviations: Probes follow Selectivity Estimation (17 x 17 grid of dynamic Gaussian white noise on uniform gray; full-field drifting gratings at the basis set's six spatial frequencies, three temporal frequencies and eight directions; response minus the response to gray). The paper does not give the noise or grating contrast, the gray level or the probe duration; the standard choices are L* 50 gray, noise s.d. 25 L*, grating amplitude 40 L*, 40 frames of which the middle 20 are scored. The predicted response to a sustained probe is its features times the directional weights (penalty reading a) summed over the four delays. The Gaussian is isotropic, fit by a search over centers (half-cell steps, also outside the display) and widths with amplitude and offset by least squares.
The fits of fig2de-prediction-accuracy (ridge in place of L1), under penalty reading a.

outcomes.statement: For subject S1 the motion-energy model identifies the test second that evoked an observed BOLD pattern within one volume (1 s) 95% of the time (464 of 486 volumes), far above chance (under 1%, 3 of 486).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 9; Figures 3A and 3B with legends
outcomes.quote: Our motion-energy encoding model could identify the specific movie stimulus that evoked an observed BOLD signal 95% of the time (464 of 486 volumes) within 6 one volume (1 s; subject S1; Figures 3A and 3B)
outcomes.notes: With the four-delay directional model (reading a), the repeat-averaged test signal (reading i), the encoding penalties of reading b (five-fold cross-validation), the 2,000 voxels best predicted on the held-out training data, and the Tikhonov penalty chosen on the held-out training data (5.623 times the mean residual variance; 506 of 728 held-out samples identified within 1 s), 426 of 486 test volumes (87.7%) are identified within one volume, at least the 418 the tolerance needs, and 38 short of 464. Chance is 2.96 of 486 (0.61%). Over the Tikhonov grid the counts run from 319 to 432; penalties 1 to 5.623 all give 424 to 432, and the best on the test data (3.162, 432) is not the one chosen. Single repeats give 360.4 on average (344 to 390). The reading b penalties come from cross-validation over all 7,128 training samples, so the held-out 728 samples that choose the voxels and the Tikhonov penalty also took part in choosing each voxel's encoding penalty; no test data is involved. With encoding penalty reading a, the same model and signal give 408 of 486 (84.0%), 10 short of the tolerance (Tikhonov penalty 3.162; 521 of 728 held-out samples). No Tikhonov penalty of the grid (0.1 to 100, quarter decades) reaches 418 under that reading; the counts run from 313 to 408. Single repeats give 337.3 on average (320 to 364); the single 4 s delay model gives 326 (repeat mean) and 231.5 (single repeats), both under reading a. An earlier run of the same code gave 409 under reading a, so counts move by about one between runs from floating-point differences. The round-1 count of 424 came from a different analysis (a held-out split drawn per subject, a ridge grid of 10 to 1e7, and the zero-spatial-frequency filters summed in the nondirectional model), so its difference from 408 cannot be put down to the split alone.
deviations: The fits use ridge regression in place of L1 (see fig2de-prediction-accuracy), under penalty readings a and b; the outcome rests on reading b, under which the 90% fit for voxel selection and the Tikhonov choice uses the reading b penalties.

The Tikhonov inverse is inv(S + lambda * mean(diag S) * I), lambda from 0.1 to 100 in quarter decades, chosen by identification of the held-out 10% of the training data with the residual covariance of the 90% fit (claims file, Likelihood). The scaling by the mean residual variance is a standard choice.
Test volumes are compared with all 486 candidate test seconds; within one volume means within 1 s on the 540 s test clock.

outcomes.statement: Identification accuracy within one volume stays above 75% for all three subjects even when the candidate set holds 1,000,000 clips drawn at random from the internet.
outcomes.quote: Identification accuracy (within 6 one volume) was >75% for all three subjects even when the set of possible natural movie clips included 1,000,000 separate clips chosen at random from the internet
outcomes.notes: Needs a set of 1,000,000 1 s clips from the internet. The data set holds only the experiment's stimuli (data descriptor and bucket listing of vim-2), and the paper names no location for the clips (Results paragraph 9, Figure 3C legend). The training movies (about 7,128 s) could serve as distractors for a partial test, but not at the 1,000,000 clips the criterion names; it was not run.

outcomes.statement: Bayesian decoding with a sampled prior of about 18,000,000 s of internet movies reconstructs the viewed movies; the maximum a posteriori (MAP) clip is good when the prior holds similar clips and poor otherwise, and the average of the 100 highest posterior clips (AHP) captures the spatiotemporal structure even of unique clips.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraphs 10 and 11; Figure 4A to 4C with legend; Figure S2
outcomes.quote: When the sampled natural movie prior contained clips similar to the viewed clip, the MAP reconstructions were good ... However, when the prior contained no clips similar to the viewed clip, the reconstructions are poor ... The AHP reconstruction captures the spatiotemporal structure within a viewed clip even when it is completely unique
outcomes.notes: Needs the sampled prior of about 18,000,000 s of YouTube clips, which the data set does not hold (bucket listing of vim-2) and the paper does not deposit or locate (Results paragraph 10, Figure S2 legend).

outcomes.statement: For all three subjects both MAP and AHP reconstructions correlate with the viewed movies in motion-energy space above chance (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p < 0.0001), and AHP reconstructions are better than MAP (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.0001), though still crude (motion-energy correlation about 0.3).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 12; Figure 4D with legend; Supplemental Experimental Procedures, Evaluating the Accuracy of Reconstructions
outcomes.quote: In both cases, reconstruction accuracy was significantly higher than chance (p < 0.0001, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; see Supplemental Experimental Procedures). Furthermore, AHP reconstructions were significantly better than MAP reconstructions (p < 0.0001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).

statistics.about: MAP and AHP reconstructions against random prior clips
statistics.n: 1 s test clips, each of three subjects
1 s test clips, each of three subjects

outcomes.notes: Needs the sampled prior, as fig4-reconstructions.

outcomes.statement: In preliminary work, encoding models with explicit color information did not predict or identify better than models using luminance alone.
outcomes.quote: However, we found that color information did not improve the accuracy of predictions or identification beyond what could be achieved with models that include only luminance information.
outcomes.notes: The color model (the directional bank applied to L*, A* and B*, 78,660 regressors) predicts worse than the luminance model, not better. Pooled over 13,007 voxels, penalty reading a, mean accuracy 0.3640 against 0.3735 (difference -0.0095, repeat-averaged signal; -0.0047 for single repeats), lower in every subject (-0.0073, -0.0082, -0.0128), better in 38% of voxels; the one-sided Wilcoxon test of color greater gives p = 1.0, so color is not higher by the test. Penalty reading b gives 0.3756 against 0.3861 (-0.0105; single repeats -0.0052), lower in every subject, one-sided p = 1.0. With a separate weight per color channel (banded ridge; weights 0, 0.1, 0.3 and 1 in eight pairs, luminance alone among them, chosen per voxel with the penalty on the held-out data), 2,674, 3,295 and 3,222 voxels choose some color, but the banded model gives 0.3669 against 0.3735 (-0.0066), lower in every subject and in the voxels that chose color, one-sided p = 1.0. S1 identification, reported without a test, gives 378 of 486 for color against 408 for luminance. The outcome rests on the claims file's reading of the color model and on ridge regression; the shared penalty is not what makes the color model worse.
deviations: The fits use ridge regression in place of L1 (see fig2de-prediction-accuracy), under penalty readings a and b; the banded check under reading a only, for time.
Each channel's features are z-scored with their own training statistics before the channels are joined (standard choice).
Run in a second notebook, color_no_gain.ipynb, as the three filterings with the other analyses would pass the hour a notebook may take.

findings.statement: The data descriptor does not say that the responses include the first 6 s of each 600 s training run (and of each 60 s test block) that the paper discards for the onset transient. They do; the mean training response over those seconds is 0.42, 0.41 and 0.28 in the three subjects, against 0.01 over the other samples.

The descriptor does not give the units of the test responses. rt is z-scored per run (s.d. 0.99), while rv and rva have s.d. 0.10 to 0.11 and 0.20 to 0.23, so the test responses are on another scale; a likelihood that uses training residuals needs them rescaled.
The descriptor does not say that some voxels hold missing values; 179, 46 and 29 of the V1 to V3B voxels of S1, S2 and S3 have missing training or test values.

The descriptor says peak BOLD responses to each timepoint were estimated, which could be read as responses already aligned to the stimulus. They are not; the directional model at a single delay predicts the test data with mean accuracy 0.06 to 0.09 at 0 s, 0.30 to 0.33 at 4 s and 0.13 to 0.15 at 8 s, so the hemodynamic delay is still in the data.

The files hold many ROI masks beyond V1 to V3B, by hemisphere, and the set differs between subjects (30 masks in S1, among them V4, MT, MTp, IP, OBJ, VO, FFA, empty on the left, and PPA, empty on both sides; 30 in S2, among them EBA, OFA and V7; 44 in S3, among them IPS1 to IPS4, MST, TOS and cortALL). The descriptor names only one by example and does not say how they were defined. One subject 3 voxel lies in two of the V1 to V3B masks.

The sampled natural movie prior (about 18,000,000 s of YouTube clips), the 1,000,000-clip identification set and the multifocal retinotopic mapping data are not in the data set and not public, so the reconstruction findings of Figure 4 and the large-set identification of Figure 3C cannot be tested, and the receptive-field maps can be judged only on a proxy.

paper_notes.statement: The paper fits each voxel by L1-regularized least squares by coordinate descent (refs. 15 and 16) but does not say how the penalty or the stopping point was chosen, and publishes no code. Here ridge is used, with the penalty chosen per voxel on held-out training data, and the static model's mean accuracy is within tolerance under five-fold cross-validation (0.233) but not under a single held-out 10% (0.211); an approximate L1 fit on 120 voxels predicts better than ridge by 0.005 to 0.025. Was the penalty chosen per voxel on held-out training data, and on which split?

The paper does not say whether identification and prediction accuracy use the mean of the ten test repeats or single repeats, nor how the Tikhonov penalty of the noise covariance was chosen. Here the repeat mean with a Tikhonov penalty chosen on held-out training data gives 408 of 486 with encoding penalties chosen on one held-out 10% and 426 with penalties chosen by five-fold cross-validation, below the reported 464; were these the choices, and how were the encoding penalties chosen for identification?
